claims.text: Increasing the density of defective T-graphite anchoring sites on carbon-coated CeO2 nanorods will enhance anchoring of sub-nanometric CoNiCuZnPd clusters.
Strong support–cluster anchoring restricts atomic mobility.
Strong support–cluster anchoring suppresses cluster coalescence.
Restricted atomic mobility and coalescence preserve a single-phase solid solution during cyclic thermal and redox exposure.
The proposed material consists of sub-nanometric CoNiCuZnPd clusters supported on carbon-coated CeO2 nanorods.
In situ Joule-heating synthesis can be used to deliberately vary the defect density of the T-graphite-like support layer.
Electron energy-loss spectroscopy can quantitatively calibrate the relevant T-graphite defect levels.
Defective turbostratic graphite sites are the structural mediator at the support–nanoparticle interface.
Defect sites provide strong, localized anchoring of the alloy clusters.
Defect-mediated anchoring reduces elemental segregation during high-temperature cyclic stress.
High-defect-density supports will produce less cluster coarsening than low-defect-density supports after identical cycling.
High-defect-density supports will retain a more uniform equiatomic elemental distribution than low-defect-density supports after identical cycling.
High-defect-density supports will improve structural stability relative to low-defect-density supports.
Clusters on supports with few defective T-graphite sites will have higher atomic mobility under the same conditions.
Clusters on supports with few defective T-graphite sites will undergo more coalescence and elemental segregation.
The proposed mechanism is limited to sub-nanometric CoNiCuZnPd clusters on carbon-coated CeO2 supports containing T-graphite structures.
Applicability to other particle sizes, compositions, and support materials is uncertain.
A lack of statistically significant improvement in both coarsening resistance and compositional uniformity for the high-defect group would falsify the hypothesis.
